name: Freyr's Sword
aliases: The Sword That Fights by Itself
powers: Fights of its own accord, without a hand to wield it.
description: The self-fighting sword of Freyr, which he gave to his servant Skírnir as payment for wooing the giantess Gerðr on his behalf. Stripped of his blade, Freyr was weaponless when the fire giant Surtr faced him at Ragnarök, and he fell. The sword is remembered in the Eddas as the price of love and the cause of a god's death.

name: Freyja's Falcon Cloak
powers: Lets its wearer fly in the shape of a falcon.
description: The falcon cloak of the goddess Freyja, a feather garment that lets its wearer fly in the shape of a falcon. Loki borrows it to fetch the goddess Iðunn back from the giant Þjazi, and later to pursue the giant in the same form. In the Prose Edda the cloak is the gods' regular means of swift flight, kept in Freyja's keeping.

name: Swedish Folk Costume
material: Wool and linen with silver and embroidery
description: The Swedish folk costume (folkdräkt), the regional dress of parish and province, worn for work and festivals and gradually codified from the 18th century. Each district had its own colours, cut, embroidery, and accessories such as the flounced apron and the bodice. The national costume, the Sverigedräkt, was created in 1903 by Märta Jörgensen and has since been widely adopted.

name: The Flower of Happiness
maker: Grows at Sunnymount Crest in the tale
powers: Possessing it was said to bring happiness.
description: The flower of happiness, the marvel of a tale told at Sunnymount Crest: a flower whose possession, or whose bloom, was said to bring happiness to whoever found it. In the tale the search for the flower tests the seeker, and the happiness it brings is measured in the finding. The flower is an object-lesson of the wonder-tale rather than a real plant.

name: The Flying Trunk
powers: Carries its owner through the air to wherever he wishes.
description: The enchanted wooden trunk of Andersen's tale, given to a spendthrift merchant's son by a rich merchant and used by its owner to fly to the land of the Turks and court a princess. When he squanders his last coins on fireworks, the sparks set the trunk alight and it burns to ash, leaving him to wander. The tale plays the magic object as both luck and ruin.
source: Hans Christian Andersen, Den flyvende kuffert (1839)

name: Ship of the Flying Dutchman
powers: Doomed to sail the Cape of Good Hope forever; sighting it is an omen.
description: The ghost ship of the Flying Dutchman, a spectral East Indiaman doomed to round the Cape of Good Hope forever after its captain, variously named Van der Decken, swore against the wind in a storm. Sightings were reported from the seventeenth century onward; no physical vessel exists, and the tale is maritime legend.
source: Maritime legend, from the seventeenth century

name: Frau Holle's Feather Bed
powers: Shaken by Frau Holle, its feathers fall to earth as snow.
description: Frau Holle's feather bed, the great bedding the old woman shakes in the Grimm tale of the same name. Each time she shakes it the feathers fall as snow, which is why, the tale explains, snow falls in winter. The heroine earns it through service; the episode is the story's comic explanation of the seasons.

name: Franks Casket
description: The Franks Casket, an eighth-century Anglo-Saxon chest carved from whalebone, covered with scenes from Germanic legend, the Bible and classical history, with runic and Latin inscriptions. The front panel shows the smith Weland being released by a maiden he rescued. It was bought in the nineteenth century and is now in the British Museum.

name: The Feather of Ma'at
powers: The counterweight of truth against which the heart of the dead is weighed.
description: The ostrich feather worn on the head of the goddess Ma'at, placed on the scales of judgment as the counterweight to the heart of the dead. A heart lighter than the feather passed on to the afterlife; a heavier one was devoured by Ammit. The feather, also worn by the god Shu in his role of lifting the sky, became the emblem of a life measured by truth.

name: Flaming Pearl
description: A luminous pearl wreathed in flame (huozhu) depicted in Chinese art as the treasure two dragons chase or guard. Linked to the dragon's undersea realm and to Buddhist wish-granting jewels, the flaming pearl symbolizes wisdom, wealth, and transformation, and it appears on temple roofs, ceramics, and paintings across East Asia.
source: Dragon art motif; Buddhist jewel tradition

name: The Four White Umbrellas
powers: Emblems of the right to rule granted from above
description: The white-tiered umbrellas that the Burmese chronicles place among the regalia of the first kings, emblems of the right to rule granted from above. Their role in the creation tale of kingship binds earthly sovereignty to the nats, and umbrella standards still crown Burmese pagodas and throne halls as marks of sacred authority.

name: False Face Mask
material: Carved basswood with red and black paint
powers: Wards off sickness with the power of the forest spirits.
description: A distorted human face carved from living basswood, painted red and black, used by the Haudenosaunee False Face Society in curing ceremonies that drive sickness away. The twisted faces recall the forest being who broke his face in a contest with the sun and gained power over disease. Sacred, handled only by society members, the masks are cut from the living tree without metal.

name: Fon Asen Altar Staff
description: Asen are commemorative altar staffs of the Fon of Benin (Dahomey), forged iron poles topped by figurative scenes - ancestor portraits, animals, or scenes of daily life - set in clay or iron bases. Placed by the ancestor altar of the compound, they receive offerings during family rites and keep the dead present in Vodun practice.
source: Fon ancestor ritual; museum collections (Musée du quai Branly)

name: Fijian Masi (Barkcloth)
description: Barkcloth of Fiji, beaten from the inner bark of the paper mulberry and painted with geometric designs in black and brown. Masi is made by women for gifts, ceremony and dress, and the finest pieces are given at weddings and installed in the chiefly house, where their patterns record the clan and its history.
source: Ethnographic records of Fijian material culture

name: Fijian War Club
description: Carved club of the Fijian islands, shaped in a range of forms from long straight blades to bulbous knobs, and often ornamented with incised patterns. War clubs were the emblem of the Fijian warrior and were also used as badges of rank, passed down as trophies and treasures, with some weapons bearing a name and the history of their owners.

name: Fujara
description: The fujara is a long overtone flute of Slovak shepherds, up to two metres long, made from elder or maple wood with a unique air duct. Played while standing, it produces a deep humming bass; its sound and technique were inscribed by UNESCO in 2008 as a living shepherd tradition.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Slovak ethnomusicology

name: Firebird's Feather
description: Golden feather of the Firebird (Zhar-ptitsa) of Russian fairy tales, which shines so brightly that it lights a whole dark room and is carried by heroes such as Ivan Tsarevich into the tsar's palace. In Afanasyev's tale the feather, and later the bird itself, is sought as a task set by the tsar; the radiant Firebird became a favourite motif of Russian decorative art.
